Returns an access token whose subject is the target user and whose actor is the caller; every action taken with it is attributed to both.

get.description:
A hypervisor in a managed estate has no route to the internet, so the control plane is the only host it can fetch a new agent from. Without this an upgrade means copying a binary to every machine by hand, which is how a fleet ends up running four different versions.

An EMPTY build list is not a failure. A server compiled without agent binaries is an ordinary development build, and an agent reads it as nothing to do.
get.summary: What agent binaries this control plane can serve

get.description:
Authenticated, even though the same bytes sit in the SPA's embedded tree. Serving them as a static asset would hand the fleet's agent binary to anyone who could reach the login page.

Verify the response against the sha256 from /agent/dist before running it.
get.summary: Download the agent binary for one platform

post.description: Redeems an enrolment token and returns this host's agent-scoped key and secret. The host is admitted into an ORGANIZATION, not a fleet — joining one is a task, so a new host and a host migrating between fleets follow the same path. Idempotent on machine_id: a rebuilt hypervisor re-enrols onto the same MACHINE record with a fresh credential rather than leaving a permanently-offline ghost. A machine a capacity sync has already discovered in a cluster is adopted rather than duplicated, matched by the node name its hostname implies.
post.summary: Enrol a fleet agent into an organization

get.description:
The complete nft ruleset, not a patch — it begins with a flush, so a host that missed several revisions converges on this one rather than replaying a history it never saw.

An EMPTY response means hold what you have. It is returned for a machine in no fleet and for a fleet that has published nothing, and neither is an empty ruleset: flushing there would strip a host of its management access at the moment it is least reachable. Separate from the heartbeat because the body can be tens of kilobytes and would otherwise ride on every poll from every host to say 'unchanged'.
get.summary: Fetch the ruleset this host should enforce

post.description: One request carries both, deliberately: two endpoints would give a bee two ways to be 'seen', and a bee parked on a long poll would have to heartbeat separately to avoid looking dead. Declare unavailable_for_seconds BEFORE doing anything that interrupts the host — a reboot is indistinguishable from a failure unless the host says in advance that it is coming back.

get.description:
The COMPLETE desired composition, not a delta. A node present in the cluster and absent from this list is desired-absent, which is what a departure looks like from the outside.

Published per CLUSTER rather than per host, because a departure is executed by a node that REMAINS: the node being removed cannot run delnode against itself. An agent that only knew its own membership could never own that, so every member is told the whole composition and reconciles its own view of it.

The agent derives the verb from this against what corosync reports — to become a member of a cluster with no other members is create, of one with members is join, and of nothing is delnode. Nothing here decides which.

An EMPTY response means hold what you have. It is returned for a machine in no hive and for a hive that has published nothing, and neither is an instruction to leave a cluster.
get.summary: Fetch the cluster composition this host's hive should have

post.description: So a fleet operation can be watched without SSH-ing to a hypervisor mid-rotation, which during an evacuation is often the one thing you must not do. Lines carry a per-task sequence assigned by the bee; resending a batch is a no-op.
post.summary: Stream task output back to the control plane

post.description: Terminal reports are idempotent. A bee that finishes and dies before its report is acknowledged will report again on restart, and rejecting the duplicate would strand the task against a host that considers it done.
post.summary: Report progress or the outcome of a task

get.description: Your own user-scoped keys, plus the organization's org-scoped keys. Never returns key or secret material: only hashes are stored, and a key that is lost is replaced rather than recovered. Agent keys are not listed — they belong to the fleet surface.

post.description:
Returns the plaintext credential ONCE. Only its hash is stored, so a key that is not captured from this response is replaced rather than recovered — no endpoint reissues or reveals one.

A user-scoped key needs nothing beyond membership: it acts as you and can do nothing you cannot. An org-scoped key is standing access to the whole tenant, so it requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions — an operator acting as a user must not be able to leave themselves a way back in. Agent-scoped keys are refused outright; they are issued only by fleet enrolment.

delete.description: Revocation is permanent and takes effect on the next request the key makes. You may revoke your own user-scoped keys. Revoking one of the organization's org-scoped keys requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions, for the same reason minting one does: it changes the tenant's standing access, and that has to be attributable to a real admin. Nobody may revoke another person's user key.

get.description:
Every action taken inside this organization's boundary, newest first: who took it, what it was done to, and whether it was allowed.

REFUSALS ARE RECORDED TOO. Someone who tried to depart a node and was told no is a different fact from someone who never tried, and only one of them appears in the result of the action.

The principal is not always a person. An organization API key authenticates a tenant rather than a human, and its actions are recorded against the key — so that 'automation did this' and 'nobody knows who did this' never look the same here.

post.description: Sends a password reset link if the address belongs to an active account. The response is identical either way.
Validates email and password, selects the user's organization, and returns JWT access and refresh tokens.
Revokes the current token session.
Validates an MFA pending token and TOTP code, then returns full access/refresh tokens.
Starts the WebAuthn discoverable login flow. Returns options and a signed challenge.
Validates the WebAuthn assertion and returns access/refresh tokens.

REACHABLE BEFORE POLICY IS SATISFIED. A session that has authenticated but not yet met a policy such as require_mfa can call this — that is the point, since the endpoint exists to let someone comply. Authentication still applies in full; only authorization is relaxed, and only for accounts holding NO verified factor. An account that already has one must present it first, or a stolen password could add its own authenticator. Starts the WebAuthn registration flow. Returns creation options and a signed challenge.

REACHABLE BEFORE POLICY IS SATISFIED. A session that has authenticated but not yet met a policy such as require_mfa can call this — that is the point, since the endpoint exists to let someone comply. Authentication still applies in full; only authorization is relaxed, and only for accounts holding NO verified factor. An account that already has one must present it first, or a stolen password could add its own authenticator. Validates the WebAuthn attestation and stores the credential.

get.description: Returns all passkeys registered for the authenticated user.

delete.description: Deletes a registered passkey. If no MFA methods remain, MFA is disabled.

post.description: Validates a refresh token and returns a new access and refresh token pair.

Creates the user, an organization, and the owner membership binding them — all in one transaction, because a user with no organization cannot sign in at all. Returns NO tokens: the address must be confirmed first, and confirming issues no session either — sign in through /auth/login afterwards. The organization's tenant database is not provisioned until the address is confirmed, so an unconfirmed signup costs a row and nothing else.
post.summary: Create an account and its first organization

post.description: Always answers 202, whatever the address. An unauthenticated endpoint that answered differently for a registered address than an unregistered one would be a membership oracle. Sending is throttled per account.
Consumes a single-use reset token, sets the new password, and revokes every existing session for the account.

delete.description: Disables TOTP MFA. Requires the user's password or a valid TOTP code for verification.

post.description: REACHABLE BEFORE POLICY IS SATISFIED. A session that has authenticated but not yet met a policy such as require_mfa can call this — that is the point, since the endpoint exists to let someone comply. Authentication still applies in full; only authorization is relaxed, and only for accounts holding NO verified factor. An account that already has one must present it first, or a stolen password could add its own authenticator. Generates a new TOTP secret and returns the otpauth URI for QR code rendering.

REACHABLE BEFORE POLICY IS SATISFIED. A session that has authenticated but not yet met a policy such as require_mfa can call this — that is the point, since the endpoint exists to let someone comply. Authentication still applies in full; only authorization is relaxed, and only for accounts holding NO verified factor. An account that already has one must present it first, or a stolen password could add its own authenticator. Confirms TOTP setup by validating a code. This activates MFA for the user.

Redeems the token from a confirmation link. This is what releases provisioning of the organization's tenant database — registration deliberately creates nothing but rows until an address is confirmed. No session is issued: sign in through /auth/login afterwards.

post.description: Creates the credential and the estate that binds it, atomically. Requires admin. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to install a credential they could later use.

delete.description: Removes both. Deleting only the estate would leave a sealed credential nothing references — unreachable through the API and still live at the provider.

post.description: Replaces the sealed material in place, keeping the binding. The fingerprint changes, which is how the rotation is confirmed.

get.description: Which rulesets apply where, in render order — lowest priority first. Bindings without a fleet are org-wide.

post.summary: Bind a ruleset to a fleet, or to the whole organization

put.description:
Priority and enabled are always applied. Scope is applied only when the request carries one — omitting it leaves the binding where it is, so a client that knows nothing about scope cannot widen a fleet binding to the whole organization by accident.

Moving a binding onto a scope where the same ruleset is already bound is refused: the ruleset would render twice, duplicating every rule in it.
put.summary: Reprioritise, disable, or re-scope a binding

post.description:
Renders every binding that applies to this fleet into one nft ruleset, stores it, and points the fleet at it. Bees converge on their next heartbeat.

Publishing an UNCHANGED policy does nothing and says so. Every revision makes the whole fleet re-apply, and re-applying an identical ruleset flushes and reloads every host's firewall to arrive at the state it was already in.
post.summary: Publish this fleet's rules as the next revision

post.description:
Publishes an OLD revision's body as a NEW revision. The number goes up, never down: a bee decides whether to converge by comparing what it applied against this number, and a number that moved backwards leaves a host pinned to the very ruleset being backed out.

The old body verbatim, not a re-render of the old rules — the rules have moved on, which is why this is a backout.

get.description: Newest first. This is what a backout is chosen from, so it carries the reason each revision was published and which revision a backout reproduced.
The exact text a host loads, so it can be compared against `nft list ruleset` on the machine. That comparison is the only way to answer 'is this host running what we think' from the host itself.

The flattened, ordered result of every binding that applies — org-wide and fleet-specific together. Composition is invisible from any single screen: editing one ruleset cannot show it interleaving with another, and binding priority outranks the positions being edited. Omit hive_id to see what a host belonging to NO fleet receives.

put.description: The whole rule, every time. A partial update could apply a new port against the old action, producing a rule nobody intended.

get.description: Named groups of rules. Fleets are bound to these rather than owning rules directly, so a rule an organization wants everywhere is written once instead of copied per fleet.

delete.description: Removes its rules and every binding to it. A binding to a ruleset that no longer exists would render nothing while still listing as though a fleet were covered.

get.description: Returned in the order they render within this ruleset. Order is the policy — an accept above a drop is a different rule from the reverse.

post.description: Refused if the rule cannot mean what it says — a port on a protocol that has none is dropped when rendered, so the stored rule would be wider than the one written.
post.summary: Add a rule to a ruleset

get.description: Named address lists. A rule referencing a set matches every element in it, so four management addresses across two ports is two rules and one set rather than eight rules — and adding an address is one element, not two more rules.

delete.description: Refused while a rule still references it. nft rejects a ruleset naming a set it has never heard of, and it rejects the WHOLE file — so a dangling reference would leave the host with no firewall at all rather than one missing a line.

put.description: Name and description only. A set's family decides the nft type its elements are declared as, so changing it would reinterpret every element already in it and every rule written against it.

post.description: Validated against the SET's family, not on its own: an ipv6 element in an ipv4 set renders a declaration nft rejects, and nft rejects the whole ruleset over one bad line.

delete.summary: Remove an address from a set

get.description:
Read only. Flags are set by platform staff; this says what applies here and which level decided it.

Every declared flag appears, including the ones nobody has overridden — a flag missing from this list would be indistinguishable from one that is switched off.
get.summary: The feature flags in effect for this organization

get.description:
Unauthenticated, and only the flags explicitly marked public — which today is which sign-in methods this installation offers.

NOT A VIEW OF THE FLAG SYSTEM. It carries a key and a value and nothing else: no source, no scope, no built-in default. Those describe how the installation is configured rather than what it offers, and an anonymous caller has no business knowing whether a value was set deliberately or inherited.

Organization-scoped flags never appear here at any value. They resolve differently per tenant and an anonymous caller has no tenant, so publishing one would either leak another organization's configuration or answer with a value true for nobody.
get.summary: The flags a sign-in page needs before anyone has signed in

get.description:
Every agent task, newest first: which machine ran it, what it was, whether it finished, and the agent's own account of what stopped it.

DISTINCT FROM THE AUDIT TRAIL, which records what PEOPLE did. An operator asking for a departure is one event there; the work that follows on the host is several here, and a departure that was requested successfully and then failed on the machine appears as a success in one and a failure in the other.

A failure is kept as the agent wrote it. These messages are written to be acted on — "pve-root-ca.srl is still byte-identical to the copy this node left the hive with" — and paraphrasing one loses the half that says what to do.

get.summary: What the fleet's agents have been asked to do, and what came of it

post.description:
Queues one upgrade task per agent. Each host downloads the binary this control plane serves, verifies it against the advertised digest, proves it runs, keeps the previous one, and restarts.

ROLLING BY CONSTRUCTION: a bee may hold at most one task, so no host does two things at once. Hosts do proceed in parallel with each other, which is safe here because an agent is not in the data path of anything it manages — an agent that fails to come back costs control of that host, not its guests.

Agents already on the target version, offline, or holding another task are SKIPPED and each says why. Queueing an offline agent would hand it a task it collects whenever it returns, which is often during the next incident.
post.summary: Upgrade every agent in a fleet

delete.description:
Revokes this agent's credential and then deletes its record. The MACHINE survives as agentless — its cluster membership, address and onboarding history are on the hypervisor record, not on the agent — so this is 'remove the agent', never 'forget the box'.

The credential is revoked FIRST and the revocation is verified before anything is deleted. It lives in the control database while the agent record lives in the tenant database, so no transaction covers both: deleting first and failing to revoke would leave a live agent key with nothing pointing at it, and nothing lists agent-scoped keys.

Refused with 409 while an onboarding worker holds a lease on this machine — it is installing and enrolling right now, and would either race the delete or resurrect the record behind it.

The agent process on the host is NOT stopped. It keeps running and starts failing authentication, which is the intended outcome: the credential is what this revokes.

post.description:
Admits a host into the ORGANIZATION, not into a cluster. Joining one is a task, so a brand-new host starts in the same fleetless state a migrating host passes through — which means an agent can be provisioned before any cluster exists.

Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as somebody else must not be able to mint something that admits a machine to the fleet.

get.description:
Machines with no hive: onboarded but not yet joined to a cluster, or departed from one. Every migration passes through this state and a failed arrival leaves a machine sitting in it.

Each entry carries its onboarding state, because a machine that has not finished onboarding has no agent and an arrival pointed at it will fail at the SSH.
get.summary: List machines belonging to no hive

post.description:
Records that this machine SHOULD be a member of that hive. Its own agent converges on it — no SSH, and nothing is dispatched.

The agent derives what to do from the world rather than being told: to become a member of a cluster with no other members is create, of one that has members is join. Arrival and bootstrap are therefore the same request.

Refused with 409 and reason codes when the host already belongs to a hive or still carries guests. The gate is here, on the WRITE of desired state, so a refusal is sticky: it never becomes desired state at all.
post.summary: Add a standalone machine to a hive

post.description:
Makes this host the FIRST node of a cluster that has none.

The counterpart of arrival, and the reason a new cluster can ever acquire a node: arrival refuses with target_hive_empty until a cluster has at least one member, which is every cluster on the day it is created.

Not the same operation as arriving, despite looking like it. `pvecm create` replaces nothing and is safe on a host already running guests, while `pvecm add` replaces the joining node's cluster configuration and refuses a host carrying any guest at all — so this has no guest gate and arrival does.

Refused with 409 and reason codes when the host already belongs to a cluster, when the target already has nodes (that is an arrival), or when the host has not finished onboarding.
post.summary: Create a cluster on a standalone machine

get.description: Every hive in the caller's organization, with the node count and whether a capacity sync can run for it. A hive with no API URL or credential is never synced, so every node in it reads as never-observed and every departure refuses.

delete.description:
Refuses while the cluster still holds hypervisors. A hypervisor row is the durable record of a physical machine — its machine id, its onboarding history, the agent bound to it — so deleting the cluster out from under one would either destroy that or leave it pointing at a cluster that no longer exists.

Depart the nodes first; each one becomes fleetless and keeps its identity, and the cluster can then be removed.

patch.description: Only the fields present are changed. Setting an API URL and a credential is what makes a hive syncable.

post.description:
The same job the schedule runs, enqueued immediately. Most often wanted after a departure refused with drain_unknown, which means the last observation is too stale to say whether a node is empty.

The job is unique per hive while queued or running, so asking twice gets the sync already on its way rather than a second one.
post.summary: Refresh a hive's capacity observations now

get.description:
Every MACHINE this organization owns, in a cluster or not. Each carries three independent statuses — provisioning_state (has the agent been installed), schedulable plus drain_state (may new work land here), and bee_status (is it answering right now) — because a machine can be provisioned AND cordoned AND offline at the same instant, and one badge cannot say that.

When a node cannot leave its hive, the reasons why are computed by the same gate the departure job runs, so a client never has to reimplement it. A machine in no hive reports not_a_member and appears in /fleet/fleetless as well.
get.summary: List machines with their three status axes

post.description:
Records intent for one or more machines and queues them for onboarding. The ticker claims each on its next pass, connects over SSH with the fleet key, installs the agent and enrols it.

THE HOST MUST ALREADY TRUST THE FLEET KEY. Install its public half in the host's authorized_keys first — Settings → Fleet SSH keys has the command — or every attempt fails as a refused connection.

Addresses can be pasted as a list: one per line, or separated by commas or spaces, with blank lines and #-comments ignored. Each is reported on separately, because a rack declared all-or-nothing would roll back thirty-one good hosts over one repeat.
post.summary: Bring hosts into the fleet by address

post.description: Cordoning withdraws the node from NEW placements. It does not evict anything: draining is a separate act, and conflating them would mean the only way to stop new work was to move existing work. A cordon is the first step of every departure.

Queues the departure. The host is left standalone and belonging to no fleet; it does NOT join anything. A migration is a departure and then an arrival, and the fleetless state between them is real rather than a window to hurry through.

Refused with 409 and a list of reason codes when the host is not drained, the hive is too small, or the capacity observation is too stale to decide. The gate and the departure are one transaction holding the hive's lock, so two departures from one hive are decided one after the other.
post.summary: Remove a hypervisor from its hive

post.description:
Queues the disarm as an agent task. The host destroys its copy of the hive's secrets, optionally rotates its own identity, and proves it — the control plane opens no connection.

For a machine that has ALREADY LEFT a cluster. Disarming a node that is still a member would destroy secrets it is still using, so this refuses one that is in a hive.

Ordinarily a departure queues this itself. This exists for the case where that one failed, which is exactly when a host is left holding credentials for a fleet it is no longer part of — and was, until now, the one outcome an operator could see in the fleet view and not act on.
post.summary: Destroy the cluster secrets a departed machine still holds

post.description:
Sets provisioning_state back to `pending` and clears the attempt count. This RECORDS INTENT; it does not queue a job. Onboarding is self-scheduling — a ticker claims pending rows under a lease — so there is nothing to enqueue and nothing that has to be running for the request to be meaningful.

Allowed from `failed` and from `provisioned` — the latter is 'revive', and it is safe because onboarding skips enrolment for a host that is already heartbeating, so a re-run does not invalidate a working agent's credential.

Refused with 409 while a lease is live: redriving a row a worker holds puts two workers on one host, both installing keys and reloading sshd. An EXPIRED lease is redrivable — that is the recovery path for a worker killed mid-onboard.

provisioning_error is deliberately NOT cleared. An operator watching a machine retry wants to see what it is retrying past, and it is overwritten by the next real failure.

Refused with 409 while that bee already has an outstanding task. At most one at a time is what makes 'what is this hypervisor doing' answerable from a single row.

fleet.datacenter.evict is issued to a node that will REMAIN, naming the one to remove — a node cannot remove itself from a cluster it is leaving.

get.description: Pass `since` with the highest seq already held to tail cheaply.

parameters.description: Return lines with seq greater than this. The UI polls with the highest seq it has, so a tail is one small query rather than a re-read.

schema.description: Return lines with seq greater than this. The UI polls with the highest seq it has, so a tail is one small query rather than a re-read.

post.description: Requires admin. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to invite an account they control. The organization comes from the session, never from the request.

Issues NO session. A new invitee chooses a password here and then signs in through /auth/login; an existing account gains the membership and signs in as it already could. Keeping session minting on the login path alone means lockout, MFA and the email-confirmation gate cannot be skipped by arriving through this door.

get.description: Lets the accept page render before the invitee commits to anything: which organization, which address, and whether they need to choose a password or sign in. Holding the token is the authorization — it was mailed to the address it names.

delete.description: The organization is taken from the session and used as a query predicate, so an id belonging to another tenant answers 404 rather than revoking anything.

Refused while this account is the only owner of an organization — see /me/sole-ownerships. Every session is revoked and every authentication factor removed. The record itself is retained: audit events, fleet tasks and invitations name the actor, and an audit trail that vanishes with the account is one the audited person can erase.

put.description: Change the authenticated user's password. Requires the current password.

get.description: Deleting an account is refused while it is the only owner of an organization, because that would leave a tenant nobody can administer. This names them, so the answer is actionable rather than just a refusal.
Any member may see who else is in their organization. Roles are included because they determine who to ask for access.
get.summary: List the members of this organization

delete.description: Requires admin, and an owner to remove an owner. The last owner cannot be removed.
delete.summary: Remove a member from this organization

patch.description: Requires admin, and an owner for anything crossing the owner line in either direction. The last owner cannot be demoted. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to grant themselves standing access.

get.description: Each kind shows this organization's own position AND the effective result, because 'what applies to us' is the question being asked and neither level answers it alone. A restriction merges toward strictness: the platform's floor cannot be lowered here, only raised.

put.description: Requires admin. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to change that organization's security posture under their name. Note that disabling here does NOT switch off a platform policy — a restriction merges toward strictness, so an organization can raise the floor but never lower it.
put.summary: Set a policy for this organization

get.description: Scoped to this organization. Ask before enabling — the alternative is finding out from the people who can no longer sign in.
get.summary: How many members this policy would lock out

delete.description: OWNER only, and impersonated sessions are refused. The organization stops resolving immediately: its tenant database becomes unreachable, every session scoped to it is revoked, and its agents can no longer authenticate. Key material is NOT destroyed by this call — the organization row holds the only key that can decrypt the tenant database, so erasing it would destroy the data irreversibly rather than merely retiring it. Purging is a separate operator step, which is what leaves a way back.

get.description: Every rule that gates authentication, organization creation and invitation acceptance, across every tenant. Rows written by the boot-time public-domain seed are marked, as are the ones an operator has overridden to allow — that divergence exists only in this table and nothing else reports it.

post.description: Purpose is required and has no default. Email rules beat domain rules, and among domain rules the most specific wins; anything that is not exactly 'allow' denies.

delete.description: Answers with a body rather than 204 because deleting a SEEDED rule does not last: the next boot re-creates it as a create_org deny. The response says so explicitly. Re-creating is fail-safe and stays that way — being silent about it was the problem.

put.description: Policy and reason only. Kind, value and purpose are the rule's identity — retargeting one is a delete and a create, so that both facts stay visible. This is also the durable way to permit a seeded public domain: an update survives every restart, whereas a delete is undone by the next one.

get.description:
Every flag this build declares, resolved as an organization with no override of its own would see it.

Flags are declared IN CODE. The registry names the flag; the database supplies the organization — so a key is never per-tenant, and adding a tenant adds no flags.

delete.description:
Removing a row is not the same as setting it false: the flag falls back to the default this build was written with, which is why an absent row never means off.

Clearing a flag that was not set SUCCEEDS. The requested state is reached either way.
delete.summary: Drop the installation-wide value, restoring the built-in default

put.description:
Applies to every organization that has no override of its own.

A key this build does not declare is REFUSED. That is the reason flags are registered: a free-form store accepts a mistyped key, reports success, and leaves the real flag exactly as it was.
put.summary: Set a flag for the whole installation

get.description: The question to ask before changing an installation-wide default: these are the organizations the change will NOT reach, because each has an opinion of its own.
get.summary: Which organizations have set this flag themselves

get.description:
Names and ids, so that anything targeted at one organization can be chosen rather than typed as a uuid.

Soft-deleted organizations are EXCLUDED unless asked for. A deleted tenant is not something to target, and its row survives only so a mistaken deletion can be seen and undone.

Carries no credential material of any kind. An organization row also holds the sealed connection string and tenant key that decrypt that customer's database; those columns are never read by this query.

parameters.description: Include soft-deleted organizations. Off by default: a deleted tenant is not something to target.

delete.description: The organization falls back to the installation-wide value, or to the built-in default.

put.description:
This is how a flag is targeted at one tenant. The organization is the ROW, never part of the key — so a tenant rename rewrites nothing, and 'which tenants have this on' is a query rather than a pattern match.

Refused for a platform-scoped flag: there is no per-tenant legacy login page.
put.summary: Set a flag for one organization

get.description: Every policy kind, whether or not the platform has an opinion on it. A kind the platform has never set reads as 'inherit', which is the identity element of the merge.

delete.description: Deleting is how the platform withdraws its opinion. That is NOT the same as disabling: a disabled policy contributes nothing to the merge either, but it is a stated position, and the distinction is what an organization sees when deciding whether it needs its own.
delete.summary: Return a platform policy to inherit

put.description: Impersonated sessions are refused: a platform policy applies to every tenant, and an operator acting as somebody else should not be able to change it under their name.

get.description: Ask BEFORE enabling. Turning on require_mfa across a platform where half the users have never enrolled a factor locks them out at their next request, and the only signal is a support queue.
get.summary: How many users this policy would lock out

get.description: Public halves and fingerprints. The private half is never returned by any endpoint — it is unsealed only inside a River worker, so a fleet-wide credential never passes through a response, a log or an error tracker.

post.description: Creates an Ed25519 keypair. The private half is sealed with this organization's own key and never leaves the control plane; the public half is returned in authorized_keys form for whitelisting on hypervisors. Requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions: this key opens root on every host that trusts it, and an operator acting as a customer must not be able to mint one they could later use.

delete.description: Marks the key unusable. It does NOT remove the public half from any hypervisor — that happens when the agents next converge, so a revoked key stays whitelisted on a host that is offline. The row is kept rather than deleted, so a fingerprint found in an authorized_keys file later can still be attributed to something.
